text: Which three pillars uphold empirical process control in Scrum? (Choose three.)
options: Transparency
Planning
Inspection
Adaptation
Documentation
explanation: Scrum is founded on empiricism. Its three pillars are transparency, inspection, and adaptation.

text: Which of the following are Scrum values? (Choose three.)
options: Courage
Efficiency
Focus
Velocity
Openness
explanation: The five Scrum values are commitment, focus, openness, respect, and courage. Efficiency and velocity are not Scrum values.

text: What is empiricism?
options: Making decisions based on detailed upfront planning
Asserting that knowledge comes from experience and making decisions based on what is observed
Following a fixed process defined by management
Estimating work as precisely as possible before starting
explanation: Empiricism asserts that knowledge comes from experience and that decisions are made based on what is observed.

text: Scrum is founded on which two ways of thinking?
options: Empiricism and lean thinking
Waterfall and iterative development
Kanban and extreme programming
Predictive planning and risk management
explanation: The Scrum Guide states that Scrum is founded on empiricism and lean thinking.

text: What does lean thinking contribute to Scrum?
options: It reduces waste and focuses on the essentials
It maximizes the utilization of every team member
It requires detailed documentation of all processes
It guarantees faster delivery than other approaches
explanation: Lean thinking reduces waste and focuses on the essentials.

text: How is Scrum best described?
options: A complete methodology with detailed instructions for building products
A lightweight framework that helps people, teams and organizations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems
A project management process focused on documentation
A set of mandatory engineering practices
explanation: Scrum is a lightweight framework, purposefully incomplete, that helps generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems. It is not a methodology.

text: Why is transparency important in Scrum?
options: It allows management to monitor individual performance
It enables meaningful inspection; inspection without transparency is misleading and wasteful
It replaces the need for trust within the team
It ensures the team never makes mistakes
explanation: Transparency enables inspection. Inspection without transparency is misleading and wasteful, and low-transparency artifacts can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk.

text: What is the relationship between inspection and adaptation?
options: Adaptation should happen once per release after a formal inspection
Inspection is optional if the team is experienced
Inspection without adaptation is considered pointless
Adaptation must always be approved by the Product Owner
explanation: Inspection enables adaptation. Inspection without adaptation is considered pointless.

text: Why does Scrum employ an iterative, incremental approach?
options: To deliver complete documentation at each milestone
To optimize predictability and to control risk
To ensure the team works at maximum capacity
To eliminate the need for stakeholder feedback
explanation: Scrum employs an iterative, incremental approach to optimize predictability and to control risk.

text: When should an adjustment be made if an inspection shows that an aspect of the work deviates outside acceptable limits?
options: At the next Sprint Retrospective
As soon as possible to minimize further deviation
At the end of the release
Only after approval by stakeholders
explanation: The adjustment must be made as soon as possible to minimize further deviation.

text: What happens to the Scrum framework when the team changes its core design or ideas, or leaves out elements?
options: It becomes a customized version of Scrum
It becomes more efficient
The result is not Scrum anymore
Nothing, as long as the team delivers
explanation: Changing the core design or ideas of Scrum, leaving out elements, or not following its rules covers up problems and limits the benefits of Scrum, potentially even rendering it useless. Scrum exists only in its entirety.

text: How do the Scrum values relate to trust?
options: Trust is only necessary between the Scrum Master and the Developers
When the values are embodied by the Scrum Team, the pillars come to life, building trust
Trust replaces the need for the Scrum values
Trust is established through detailed contracts
explanation: When the values of commitment, focus, openness, respect, and courage are embodied by the Scrum Team and the people they work with, the empirical pillars come to life, building trust.

text: The Scrum framework is purposefully incomplete. What does this mean?
options: Scrum is unfinished and will be completed in future versions
Scrum only defines the parts required to implement Scrum theory; it is built upon by the collective intelligence of the people using it
Teams must purchase additional modules to use Scrum fully
Scrum cannot be used without another framework
explanation: Scrum is purposefully incomplete, only defining the parts required to implement Scrum theory. Rather than providing detailed instructions, it guides relationships and interactions.

text: Which statement about the Scrum events and empiricism is correct?
options: The events are optional ceremonies that mature teams can skip
Each event is a formal opportunity to inspect and adapt Scrum artifacts
Only the Sprint Retrospective supports inspection and adaptation
The events exist mainly to report status to management
explanation: Scrum combines four formal events for inspection and adaptation within a containing event, the Sprint. Each event is a formal opportunity to inspect and adapt Scrum artifacts.

text: In which environments does Scrum work best?
options: Simple, repeatable work with predictable outcomes
Complex environments where more is unknown than known
Only software development projects
Environments with fixed requirements and stable technology
explanation: Scrum is designed for complex work where more is unknown than known and empiricism is needed to make progress.

text: Which of the following demonstrate the Scrum value of courage? (Choose two.)
options: Working on the hardest problems even when the outcome is uncertain
Hiding bad news from stakeholders to protect the team
Saying no to work that would endanger the Sprint Goal
Always agreeing with the loudest team member
explanation: The Scrum Team members have the courage to do the right thing and to work on tough problems. This includes openly addressing difficult topics and protecting the Sprint Goal.

text: Which accountabilities exist within a Scrum Team? (Choose three.)
options: Product Owner
Project Manager
Scrum Master
Developers
Team Lead
explanation: The Scrum Team consists of one Scrum Master, one Product Owner, and Developers. There are no other roles such as project manager or team lead.

text: What is the typical size of a Scrum Team?
options: Exactly 7 people
10 or fewer people
Between 15 and 20 people
As many as the project requires
explanation: The Scrum Team is small enough to remain nimble and large enough to complete significant work within a Sprint, typically 10 or fewer people.

text: What does it mean that the Scrum Team is self-managing?
options: The team decides its own salaries and vacation days
The team internally decides who does what, when, and how
The team does not need a Scrum Master
Each member manages their own separate backlog
explanation: Scrum Teams are self-managing, meaning they internally decide who does what, when, and how.

text: What does it mean that the Scrum Team is cross-functional?
options: Every member can perform every task
The members have all the skills necessary to create value each Sprint
The team works across multiple products at once
The team includes members from every department of the company
explanation: Cross-functional means the members have all the skills necessary to create value each Sprint, not that everyone can do everything.

text: Who is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team?
options: The Scrum Master
The Product Owner
The Developers
The stakeholders
explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team.

text: The Product Owner is accountable for effective Product Backlog management. Which activities does this include? (Choose three.)
options: Developing and explicitly communicating the Product Goal
Assigning Product Backlog items to individual Developers
Creating and clearly communicating Product Backlog items
Ordering Product Backlog items
Estimating the size of Product Backlog items
explanation: Product Backlog management includes developing and communicating the Product Goal, creating and communicating Product Backlog items, ordering them, and ensuring the Product Backlog is transparent and understood. Sizing is done by the Developers, and no one assigns work to Developers.

text: May the Product Owner delegate Product Backlog management work to others?
options: No, the Product Owner must do all the work personally
Yes, but the Product Owner remains accountable
Yes, and the accountability transfers to whoever does the work
Only to the Scrum Master
explanation: The Product Owner may delegate the work to others, but remains accountable.

text: How many people share the Product Owner accountability for a product?
options: One person; the Product Owner is not a committee
One per Scrum Team working on the product
A committee of stakeholders
Two, so one is always available
explanation: The Product Owner is one person, not a committee. Multiple teams working on the same product share the same Product Owner.

text: A stakeholder wants to change the Product Backlog. What should happen?
options: The stakeholder edits the Product Backlog directly
The stakeholder convinces the Developers to add the item to the Sprint
The stakeholder tries to convince the Product Owner, who decides
The Scrum Master adds the change if it seems valuable
explanation: Those wanting to change the Product Backlog can do so by trying to convince the Product Owner. For Product Owners to succeed, the entire organization must respect their decisions.

text: What is the Scrum Master accountable for? (Choose two.)
options: Establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide
The Scrum Team's effectiveness
Writing the Product Backlog items
Assigning tasks during the Sprint
explanation: The Scrum Master is accountable for establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide and for the Scrum Team's effectiveness.

text: How does the Scrum Guide describe the Scrum Master's leadership?
options: A true leader who serves the Scrum Team and the larger organization
A manager who directs the Developers' daily work
A technical lead who makes architectural decisions
A representative of management inside the team
explanation: Scrum Masters are true leaders who serve the Scrum Team and the larger organization.

text: In which ways does the Scrum Master serve the Product Owner? (Choose two.)
options: Helping find techniques for effective Product Goal definition and Product Backlog management
Ordering the Product Backlog on the Product Owner's behalf
Facilitating stakeholder collaboration as requested or needed
Approving the Product Owner's decisions
explanation: The Scrum Master serves the Product Owner by helping find techniques for Product Goal definition and Product Backlog management, helping the team understand the need for clear items, helping establish empirical product planning, and facilitating stakeholder collaboration as requested or needed.

text: How does the Scrum Master serve the larger organization? (Choose two.)
options: Leading, training, and coaching the organization in its Scrum adoption
Reporting each Developer's performance to management
Removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams
Ensuring all teams in the organization use identical practices
explanation: The Scrum Master serves the organization by leading, training, and coaching the Scrum adoption, planning and advising Scrum implementations, helping employees and stakeholders understand an empirical approach, and removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams.

text: What are the Developers accountable for? (Choose three.)
options: Creating a plan for the Sprint, the Sprint Backlog
Instilling quality by adhering to a Definition of Done
Ordering the Product Backlog
Adapting their plan each day toward the Sprint Goal
Cancelling the Sprint when needed
explanation: Developers are accountable for creating the Sprint Backlog, instilling quality via the Definition of Done, adapting their plan each day toward the Sprint Goal, and holding each other accountable as professionals. Ordering the Product Backlog is the Product Owner's job; only the Product Owner can cancel a Sprint.

text: Who is accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint?
options: The Developers
The Product Owner
The entire Scrum Team
The Scrum Master
explanation: The entire Scrum Team is accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint.

text: Several Scrum Teams work on the same product. What must they share? (Choose two.)
options: The same Product Owner
The same Scrum Master
The same Product Backlog
The same Sprint Backlog
explanation: If Scrum Teams become too large, they should reorganize into multiple cohesive Scrum Teams, each focused on the same product, sharing the same Product Goal, Product Backlog, and Product Owner. Each team has its own Sprint Backlog.

text: Who sizes (estimates) Product Backlog items?
options: The Product Owner, because they know the value
The Developers who will do the work
The Scrum Master, as a neutral party
The stakeholders
explanation: The Developers who will be doing the work are responsible for the sizing. The Product Owner may influence them by helping understand and select trade-offs.

text: Are there sub-teams or hierarchies within a Scrum Team?
options: Yes, a testing sub-team is recommended
Yes, the Scrum Master is above the Developers
No, it is a cohesive unit of professionals focused on one objective at a time, the Product Goal
Only in teams larger than 10 people
explanation: Within a Scrum Team, there are no sub-teams or hierarchies. It is a cohesive unit of professionals focused on one objective at a time, the Product Goal.

text: A Developer is repeatedly pulled away by a manager to work on tasks outside the Sprint. What should the Scrum Master do?
options: Nothing, managers outrank the Scrum Team
Coach the organization and address the impediment, protecting the team's focus
Ask the Product Owner to add the manager's tasks to the Sprint Backlog
Extend the Sprint to compensate for the lost time
explanation: The Scrum Master serves the team by causing the removal of impediments and serves the organization by helping it understand and enact an empirical approach. Interruptions that endanger the Sprint Goal are an impediment to address.

text: Who has the authority to cancel a Sprint?
options: The Scrum Master
The Developers by majority vote
Only the Product Owner
Any stakeholder
explanation: A Sprint could be cancelled if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. Only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel the Sprint.

text: What is the maximum length of a Sprint?
options: One week
Two weeks
One month
Six weeks
explanation: Sprints are the heartbeat of Scrum. They are fixed-length events of one month or less to create consistency.

text: When does a new Sprint start?
options: Immediately after the conclusion of the previous Sprint
After the Sprint Planning of the next release
One week after the Sprint Review
When the Product Owner approves the Increment
explanation: A new Sprint starts immediately after the conclusion of the previous Sprint. There are no gaps between Sprints.

text: Which events happen within the Sprint? (Choose three.)
options: Sprint Planning
Release Planning
Daily Scrum
Sprint Retrospective
Hardening Sprint
explanation: The Sprint is a container for all other events: Sprint Planning, Daily Scrums, Sprint Review, and Sprint Retrospective. Release planning and hardening sprints are not Scrum events.

text: Which of the following holds true during a Sprint? (Choose three.)
options: No changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal
Quality does not decrease
The Sprint Backlog is frozen and cannot change
The Product Backlog is refined as needed
Scope cannot be discussed until the Sprint Review
explanation: During the Sprint: no changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal, quality does not decrease, the Product Backlog is refined as needed, and scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned.

text: The Developers realize mid-Sprint that they selected too much work. What should they do?
options: Work overtime to complete everything
Lower the quality standards to finish faster
Collaborate with the Product Owner to renegotiate the scope of the Sprint Backlog without endangering the Sprint Goal
Cancel the Sprint
explanation: If the work turns out to be different than expected, the Developers collaborate with the Product Owner to negotiate the scope of the Sprint Backlog within the Sprint without affecting the Sprint Goal.

text: Why are shorter Sprints useful?
options: They generate more learning cycles and limit risk of cost and effort to a smaller time frame
They allow more meetings per month
They reduce the need for a Definition of Done
They make velocity comparisons between teams easier
explanation: When a Sprint's horizon is too long, the Sprint Goal may become invalid, complexity may rise, and risk may increase. Shorter Sprints generate more learning cycles and limit risk of cost and effort.

text: What is the timebox for Sprint Planning for a one-month Sprint?
options: Four hours
Eight hours
Two hours
One full day per week of Sprint length
explanation: Sprint Planning is timeboxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint. For shorter Sprints, the event is usually shorter.

text: Which three topics does Sprint Planning address? (Choose three.)
options: Why is this Sprint valuable?
What can be Done this Sprint?
How will the chosen work get done?
Who worked hardest last Sprint?
When will the product be finished?
explanation: Sprint Planning addresses: Why is this Sprint valuable? (Sprint Goal), What can be Done this Sprint? (selection of items), and How will the chosen work get done? (the plan).

text: When is the Sprint Goal created?
options: During the Sprint Review of the previous Sprint
During Sprint Planning, before the end of the event
During the first Daily Scrum
By the Product Owner before Sprint Planning starts
explanation: The Scrum Team collaborates to define a Sprint Goal that communicates why the Sprint is valuable to stakeholders. The Sprint Goal must be finalized prior to the end of Sprint Planning.

text: Who selects how many Product Backlog items are included in the Sprint?
options: The Product Owner
The Scrum Master
The Developers, through discussion with the Product Owner
The stakeholders based on the roadmap
explanation: Through discussion with the Product Owner, the Developers select items from the Product Backlog to include in the current Sprint. Only the Developers decide how much they can accomplish.

text: May people other than the Scrum Team attend Sprint Planning?
options: No, Sprint Planning is strictly internal
Yes, the Scrum Team may invite other people to provide advice
Yes, any stakeholder may join uninvited
Only managers may attend
explanation: The Scrum Team may invite other people to attend Sprint Planning to provide advice.

text: What is the purpose of the Daily Scrum?
options: To report progress to the Scrum Master
To inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog as necessary
To assign the day's tasks to each Developer
To update stakeholders on the project status
explanation: The purpose of the Daily Scrum is to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog as necessary, adjusting the upcoming planned work.

text: What is the timebox of the Daily Scrum, and does it depend on Sprint length?
options: 15 minutes, regardless of Sprint length
15 minutes per week of Sprint length
30 minutes for one-month Sprints
As long as the Developers need
explanation: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers, held every working day of the Sprint regardless of Sprint length.

text: Who participates in the Daily Scrum?
options: The Developers; the Product Owner and Scrum Master participate as Developers only if they are actively working on Sprint Backlog items
The entire company
The Scrum Master, who leads the meeting
The Product Owner, who checks on progress
explanation: The Daily Scrum is an event for the Developers. If the Product Owner or Scrum Master are actively working on items in the Sprint Backlog, they participate as Developers.

text: Must the Developers use the three questions (What did I do? What will I do? Any impediments?) in the Daily Scrum?
options: Yes, the Scrum Guide mandates this format
No, the Developers can select whatever structure and techniques they want, as long as it focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal
Yes, but only for new teams
No, the Scrum Master chooses the format
explanation: The Developers can select whatever structure and techniques they want, as long as their Daily Scrum focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal and produces an actionable plan for the next day of work.

text: Is the Daily Scrum the only time Developers may adjust their plan?
options: Yes, plans are locked between Daily Scrums
No, they often meet throughout the day for more detailed discussions about adapting or re-planning the rest of the Sprint's work
Yes, unless the Scrum Master allows an exception
No, but changes require Product Owner approval
explanation: The Daily Scrum is not the only time Developers are allowed to adjust their plan. They often meet throughout the day for more detailed discussions.

text: What is the purpose of the Sprint Review?
options: To inspect the outcome of the Sprint and determine future adaptations
To formally accept or reject the Increment
To demonstrate that the team worked hard
To review each Developer's individual contribution
explanation: The purpose of the Sprint Review is to inspect the outcome of the Sprint and determine future adaptations. The Scrum Team presents the results to key stakeholders and progress toward the Product Goal is discussed.

text: How does the Scrum Guide characterize the Sprint Review?
options: A working session where the Scrum Team should avoid limiting it to a presentation
A one-way demo from the Developers to stakeholders
A formal sign-off meeting with management
An internal meeting without stakeholders
explanation: The Sprint Review is a working session and the Scrum Team should avoid limiting it to a presentation. The Scrum Team and stakeholders collaborate on what to do next.

text: What is the timebox for the Sprint Review of a one-month Sprint?
options: Two hours
Three hours
Four hours
Eight hours
explanation: The Sprint Review is timeboxed to a maximum of four hours for a one-month Sprint. For shorter Sprints, the event is usually shorter.

text: What is the purpose of the Sprint Retrospective?
options: To plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness
To inspect the Increment with stakeholders
To update the Product Backlog
To evaluate the Product Owner's performance
explanation: The purpose of the Sprint Retrospective is to plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness. The team inspects how the last Sprint went with regards to individuals, interactions, processes, tools, and the Definition of Done.

text: What does the Scrum Team inspect during the Sprint Retrospective? (Choose three.)
options: Individuals and interactions
Processes and tools
The Definition of Done
The stakeholders' budget
Competitors' products
explanation: The Scrum Team inspects how the last Sprint went with regards to individuals, interactions, processes, tools, and their Definition of Done.

text: What are the timebox and position of the Sprint Retrospective?
options: Maximum three hours for a one-month Sprint; it concludes the Sprint
Maximum four hours for a one-month Sprint; it opens the Sprint
Exactly one hour, held mid-Sprint
Maximum eight hours, held after the new Sprint Planning
explanation: The Sprint Retrospective concludes the Sprint. It is timeboxed to a maximum of three hours for a one-month Sprint; for shorter Sprints it is usually shorter.

text: Why does Scrum prescribe that events are held at the same time and place?
options: To make room bookings easier
To reduce complexity
Because the Scrum Guide requires an office
To allow management to attend
explanation: Optimally, all events are held at the same time and place to reduce complexity. Events create regularity and minimize the need for meetings not defined in Scrum.

text: What happens if a Sprint is cancelled?
options: All work is discarded and the team starts over
The team takes a break until the next quarter
The remaining incomplete work returns to the Product Backlog and a new Sprint starts
The Scrum Master decides what to do with the remaining work
explanation: When a Sprint is cancelled, completed and Done work is reviewed, and incomplete Product Backlog items are re-estimated and put back on the Product Backlog. A new Sprint starts immediately.

text: Which are the three Scrum artifacts? (Choose three.)
options: Product Backlog
Burndown Chart
Sprint Backlog
Increment
Definition of Done
explanation: The three Scrum artifacts are the Product Backlog, the Sprint Backlog, and the Increment. Burndown charts are optional complementary practices; the Definition of Done is a commitment, not an artifact.

text: Each Scrum artifact contains a commitment. Which pairing is correct?
options: Product Backlog – Sprint Goal, Sprint Backlog – Product Goal, Increment – Definition of Done
Product Backlog – Product Goal, Sprint Backlog – Sprint Goal, Increment – Definition of Done
Product Backlog – Definition of Done, Sprint Backlog – Sprint Goal, Increment – Product Goal
Product Backlog – Roadmap, Sprint Backlog – Velocity, Increment – Release Plan
explanation: The commitments are: Product Goal for the Product Backlog, Sprint Goal for the Sprint Backlog, and Definition of Done for the Increment.

text: How does the Scrum Guide describe the Product Backlog?
options: A complete, fixed specification of the product
An emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product
A list of tasks assigned to Developers
A contract between the team and the stakeholders
explanation: The Product Backlog is an emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product. It is the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team.

text: What is Product Backlog refinement?
options: A mandatory event held once per Sprint
The act of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items into smaller, more precise items
The Product Owner rewriting the backlog alone each weekend
Deleting all items older than three months
explanation: Product Backlog refinement is the act of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items into smaller, more precise items. It is an ongoing activity, not a formal event.

text: What is the Product Goal?
options: The long-term objective for the Scrum Team, which lives in the Product Backlog
The list of features for the next release
A yearly target set by management
The sum of all Sprint Goals
explanation: The Product Goal describes a future state of the product and is the long-term objective for the Scrum Team. It lives in the Product Backlog.

text: How many Product Goals may a Scrum Team pursue at the same time?
options: As many as the stakeholders request
One; the team must fulfill or abandon one objective before taking on the next
One per Developer
Two: one short-term and one long-term
explanation: The Product Goal is the long-term objective for the Scrum Team. They must fulfill (or abandon) one objective before taking on the next.

text: What are the three components of the Sprint Backlog?
options: The Sprint Goal (why), the selected Product Backlog items (what), and an actionable plan for delivering the Increment (how)
The tasks, the assignees, and the deadlines
The Product Goal, the Increment, and the Definition of Done
The user stories, the acceptance criteria, and the estimates
explanation: The Sprint Backlog is composed of the Sprint Goal (why), the set of Product Backlog items selected for the Sprint (what), and an actionable plan for delivering the Increment (how).

text: Who owns and updates the Sprint Backlog?
options: The Product Owner
The Scrum Master
The Developers; it is a plan by and for them
The stakeholders
explanation: The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers. It is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned.

text: Which statements about the Increment are true? (Choose two.)
options: Each Increment is additive to all prior Increments and thoroughly verified
An Increment may only be delivered to stakeholders at the Sprint Review
Multiple Increments may be created within a single Sprint
Work that does not meet the Definition of Done may be released as a beta Increment
explanation: Each Increment is additive to all prior Increments and thoroughly verified. Multiple Increments may be created within a Sprint and may be delivered to stakeholders prior to the end of the Sprint. The Sprint Review should never be considered a gate to releasing value.

text: What happens to work that does not meet the Definition of Done by the end of the Sprint?
options: It is presented at the Sprint Review with a disclaimer
It cannot be released or presented; it returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration
It is released with known defects documented
The Sprint is extended until the work is Done
explanation: If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. Instead, it returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.

text: What is the Definition of Done?
options: A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product
A checklist the Product Owner uses to accept user stories
The acceptance criteria of a single Product Backlog item
A list of tasks that must be completed each day
explanation: The Definition of Done is a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product. The moment an item meets it, an Increment is born.

text: The organization has an official standard for the Definition of Done. What must the Scrum Team do?
options: Ignore it and create their own definition
Follow it as a minimum; the team may make it stricter
Ask management for an exception
Use it only for the final Sprint before a release
explanation: If the Definition of Done is an organizational standard, all Scrum Teams must follow it as a minimum. If it is not, the Scrum Team must create one appropriate for the product.

text: Multiple Scrum Teams work together on the same product. What applies to their Definition of Done?
options: Each team defines its own independent Definition of Done
They must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done
The Scrum Masters merge the definitions after each Sprint
Only the team releasing to production needs one
explanation: If there are multiple Scrum Teams working together on a product, they must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done.

text: Why does the Definition of Done create transparency?
options: It documents who worked on each item
It provides everyone a shared understanding of what work was completed as part of the Increment
It makes velocity public across teams
It lists the tools used during development
explanation: The Definition of Done creates transparency by providing everyone a shared understanding of what work was completed as part of the Increment.

text: What is the purpose of the Sprint Goal?
options: It lists every item that must be finished in the Sprint
It is the single objective for the Sprint that creates coherence and focus, while allowing flexibility in the exact work needed
It measures the Developers' productivity
It replaces the Product Goal during the Sprint
explanation: The Sprint Goal is the single objective for the Sprint. It creates coherence and focus and provides flexibility in terms of the exact work needed to achieve it.

text: Can the Sprint Backlog change during the Sprint?
options: No, it is fixed at Sprint Planning
Yes, the Developers update it throughout the Sprint as more is learned
Only the Product Owner may change it
Only during the Daily Scrum
explanation: The Sprint Backlog is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned. It should have enough detail that progress can be inspected in the Daily Scrum.

text: How can progress toward the Product Goal and Sprint Goal be monitored according to the Scrum Guide?
options: Burndown charts are mandatory in Scrum
Various practices exist to forecast progress, but they do not replace the importance of empiricism
Only velocity may be used
Progress tracking is the Scrum Master's private task
explanation: While various practices exist to forecast progress (like burn-downs or burn-ups), they do not replace the importance of empiricism. What will happen is unknown; only what has already happened may be used for forward-looking decision making.

text: What makes the Product Backlog the 'single source of work'?
options: Work not originating from the Product Backlog should not be undertaken by the Scrum Team
It contains the complete project plan
Only the Product Owner may read it
It is stored in a single tool
explanation: The Product Backlog is the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team. Work that does not come from it has no transparency and undermines empiricism.

text: Product Backlog items that can be Done within one Sprint are considered what?
options: Ready for selection in a Sprint Planning event
Automatically part of the next Sprint
Owned by the Scrum Master
Committed deliverables for stakeholders
explanation: Product Backlog items that can be Done by the Scrum Team within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in a Sprint Planning event. They usually acquire this transparency through refining activities.

text: When is an Increment 'born'?
options: When the Sprint ends
The moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done
When the Product Owner accepts the work at the Sprint Review
When the stakeholders approve the release
explanation: The moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done, an Increment is born. The Sprint Review is not an acceptance gate.

text: What does the Scrum value of commitment mean?
options: The Scrum Team guarantees to deliver all selected Product Backlog items
The Scrum Team commits to achieving its goals and to supporting each other
Each Developer commits to working overtime when needed
The Product Owner commits to a fixed release date
explanation: The Scrum Team commits to achieving its goals and to supporting each other. Commitment is about dedication to the team and its goals, not a guarantee of scope.

text: What does the Scrum value of focus mean?
options: Developers should not talk to stakeholders
The team's primary focus is on the work of the Sprint to make the best possible progress toward its goals
Each Developer focuses on exactly one task per day
The team focuses only on writing code
explanation: The Scrum Team's primary focus is on the work of the Sprint to make the best possible progress toward these goals.

text: What does the Scrum value of openness require?
options: The Scrum Team and its stakeholders are open about the work and the challenges
All meetings are open to the public
The source code must be open source
The team must accept every stakeholder request
explanation: The Scrum Team and its stakeholders are open about the work and the challenges.

text: What does the Scrum value of respect mean?
options: Junior members follow the decisions of senior members
Scrum Team members respect each other to be capable, independent people, and are respected as such by the people with whom they work
The team always agrees with the Product Owner
Managers are treated with special deference
explanation: Scrum Team members respect each other to be capable, independent people, and are respected as such by the people with whom they work.

text: The Developers discover a serious technical problem early in the Sprint but keep it to themselves until the Sprint Review. Which Scrum values did they fail to live? (Choose two.)
options: Openness
Focus
Courage
Respect
explanation: Being open about the work and its challenges (openness) and having the courage to raise difficult topics early would have allowed the team to inspect and adapt in time.

text: In which domains can Scrum be applied?
options: Only software development
Only IT projects
Many domains of complex work, e.g. products, services, research, schools, and government
Only projects with fewer than ten people in total
explanation: Scrum has been used extensively beyond software: for products, services, research, autonomous vehicles, schools, government, marketing, and more. It applies wherever complex work is done.

text: Why must all elements of the Scrum framework be implemented?
options: Because Scrum.org audits teams for compliance
Each element serves a specific purpose that is essential to the overall value and results realized with Scrum
Because partial Scrum is illegal
Only the events are mandatory; the artifacts are optional
explanation: Each element of the framework serves a specific purpose that is essential to the overall value and results realized with Scrum.

text: A team hides unfinished work in a hard-to-find branch so the Sprint looks successful. Which pillar of empiricism is undermined the most?
options: Transparency
Adaptation
Velocity
Commitment
explanation: Hiding the true state of the work destroys transparency. Without transparency, inspection is misleading and decisions may diminish value and increase risk.

text: Why must Scrum artifacts be transparent?
options: Because significant decisions are based on the perceived state of the artifacts
So management can track individual performance
Because auditors require it
So the artifacts can be printed for reports
explanation: Decisions to optimize value and control risk are made based on the perceived state of the artifacts. Low transparency can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk.

text: How often should Scrum artifacts and progress be inspected?
options: Once at the end of each release
Continuously by an external quality department
Frequently and diligently, but not so often that inspection gets in the way of the work
Only when problems occur
explanation: The Scrum artifacts and the progress toward agreed goals must be inspected frequently and diligently. Scrum provides cadence in the form of its five events so inspection does not get in the way of work.

text: Why are Scrum events timeboxed (given a maximum duration)?
options: To ensure an appropriate amount of time is spent without allowing waste in the process
Because meeting rooms are usually booked by the hour
To force teams to talk faster
So managers can plan their attendance
explanation: Timeboxes ensure an appropriate amount of time is spent on each event without allowing waste. Events create regularity and minimize the need for meetings not defined in Scrum.

text: Management asks for a detailed Gantt chart covering the next twelve months. What is the most Scrum-consistent response?
options: Provide the Gantt chart; Scrum requires detailed long-term plans
Explain that in complex work progress is best inspected empirically, e.g. through Done Increments and the Product Backlog
Refuse to communicate with management
Let the Scrum Master create the chart secretly
explanation: Scrum is based on empiricism: in complex environments, what will happen is unknown. Transparency comes from the artifacts and frequent inspection of real Increments, not from predictive long-term charts.

text: Is it possible to implement only parts of Scrum?
options: No, tools will prevent it
Yes, and the result is a lighter version of Scrum
Yes, it is possible, but the result is not Scrum
Only with written approval from Scrum.org
explanation: Although implementing only parts of Scrum is possible, the result is not Scrum. Scrum exists only in its entirety.

text: According to the Scrum Guide, when does adaptation become more difficult?
options: When the Sprint is shorter than two weeks
When the people involved are not empowered or self-managing
When the team uses physical task boards
When stakeholders attend the Sprint Review
explanation: Adaptation becomes more difficult when the people involved are not empowered or self-managing. A Scrum Team is expected to adapt the moment it learns anything new through inspection.

text: Which of the following is NOT one of the three pillars of empiricism?
options: Transparency
Commitment
Inspection
Adaptation
explanation: The three pillars are transparency, inspection, and adaptation. Commitment is one of the five Scrum values, not a pillar.

text: Two Developers argue about whether pair programming must be used because 'Scrum requires it'. What is true?
options: Scrum prescribes pair programming for all complex work
Scrum is a framework within which people can employ various processes and techniques; specific engineering practices are not prescribed
The Scrum Master decides which engineering practices are mandatory
Engineering practices must be approved by the Product Owner
explanation: Scrum is purposefully incomplete and does not prescribe specific engineering practices. Teams choose the processes, techniques, and methods that work best for them.

text: Why is Scrum a good fit for complex problems?
options: Because in complex work more is unknown than known, and empiricism allows learning through frequent inspection and adaptation
Because complexity can be eliminated with better upfront analysis
Because Scrum reduces the number of people involved
Because Scrum guarantees fixed scope and fixed dates
explanation: In complex environments, what will happen is unknown. Scrum's empirical, iterative-incremental approach turns this uncertainty into frequent learning cycles.

text: A stakeholder demands a fixed-scope, fixed-date plan for the next year before the team may start. What is the empirical counter-argument?
options: Scrum teams never plan
In complex work, upfront predictions are unreliable; Scrum controls risk by delivering Done Increments and adapting based on observed results
The plan should be made by the Scrum Master instead
The team should double all estimates to be safe
explanation: Scrum employs an iterative, incremental approach to optimize predictability and control risk. Forecasts are possible, but they do not replace the importance of empiricism.

text: What do the Scrum values give direction to?
options: The company's marketing strategy
The Scrum Team's work, actions, and behavior
The format of the Product Backlog
The choice of development tools
explanation: The Scrum values give direction to the Scrum Team with regard to their work, actions, and behavior. Decisions, steps taken, and the way Scrum is used should reinforce these values.

text: What does successful use of Scrum depend on?
options: Strict enforcement of the rules by management
People becoming more proficient in living the five Scrum values
Using a certified Scrum tool
Having at least one certified Scrum Master per team
explanation: Successful use of Scrum depends on people becoming more proficient in living the five values: commitment, focus, openness, respect, and courage.

text: A Developer privately disagrees with a popular technical decision but stays silent to avoid conflict. Which Scrum value would most help here?
options: Courage
Focus
Commitment
Efficiency
explanation: Scrum Team members need the courage to do the right thing and to work on tough problems, which includes voicing disagreement openly.

text: How does Scrum reduce the need for meetings not defined in the framework?
options: By forbidding all other meetings
The five events create regularity and provide formal opportunities to inspect and adapt
By making the Scrum Master attend all external meetings
By replacing communication with documentation
explanation: The events are used in Scrum to create regularity and to minimize the need for meetings not defined in Scrum.

text: What is the effect of low transparency in artifacts?
options: It has no effect as long as the team communicates verbally
Decisions based on them can diminish value and increase risk
It only affects the Scrum Master's work
It speeds up decision-making
explanation: Artifacts that have low transparency can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk.

text: Which statement about Scrum and existing practices is correct?
options: Scrum requires teams to abandon all existing practices
Scrum makes visible the relative efficacy of current management, environment, and work techniques, so that improvements can be made
Scrum certifies which practices are allowed
Existing practices automatically satisfy the Definition of Done
explanation: Scrum wraps around existing practices and makes their relative efficacy visible, so that improvements can be made.
